assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED turned a superconducting circuit into an artificial atom coupled strongly to a single microwave photon, giving dispersive readout, two-qubit gates and the architecture behind essentially all superconducting quantum processors. The idea is original, clean and has had very broad influence across quantum optics, mesoscopic physics and quantum information. This is my home field, so I weigh it with care.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff are the standard proposal and first-demonstration references; Blais (theory) with Wallraff and Schoelkopf (experiment) is a coherent three-way split of theory and strong-coupling realisation. Other contributors, such as Devoret's group and the Yale and ETH teams, make the allocation less than obvious. I may not be fully objective on how to weigh credit within this community.
assessment.maturity: Strong coupling was shown in 2004 and has been reproduced and extended in many independent laboratories for two decades; the interpretation is stable and the field is mature. Timing is a question: the 2025 prize recognised closely related circuit work, so recognition now may be seen as too soon after, even though the discoveries are distinct.
uncertainties: Overlap with, and proximity in time to, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
Exact credit among the full proposal and demonstration literature, including contributors outside the three credited names.
My own professional closeness to this subfield may bias my view; I rely only on the supplied credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution connects quantum measurement and no-cloning to provably secure communication. It is conceptually original, has launched a whole subfield of quantum cryptography, and has real devices and networks. It follows naturally after the 2022 prize for entanglement experiments.
assessment.attribution: BB84 by Bennett and Brassard is the decisive founding contribution; Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is an independent and conceptually distinct route to the same goal. All three can form a fair prize, though Ekert's share relative to BB84 is argued by some. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not in the credited names and I cannot resolve that history here.
assessment.maturity: Theory dates to the 1980s and 1990s, with many experimental demonstrations, field deployments and satellite links; the principle is thoroughly established. Practical security against side channels is still being worked on but does not undermine the physics. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Whether the physics prize or another discipline is the right home for a protocol-centred discovery.
Priority questions relating to earlier conjugate-coding proposals outside the credited names.
Practical implementation security does not match the idealised theory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction showed that fragile quantum states can be protected, and fault-tolerant computation is possible in principle. This is fundamental, original and the basis of any scalable quantum computer; as someone working on gate fidelity and processor design I see daily how central it is. The surface-code direction by Kitaev connects to topological ideas.
assessment.attribution: Shor's 1995 code and Steane's 1996 code were the first decisive constructions; Kitaev's toric code and fault-tolerance ideas are decisive on the topological and scalable side. Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and others also made major contributions and are not in the credited names, so any three-person choice leaves out important work.
assessment.maturity: Recent experiments with logical qubits and below-threshold surface-code memories give real physical confirmation, but they are early and a full fault-tolerant machine is not yet demonstrated. Recognition may be somewhat premature compared with the principle itself, which is long established theoretically.
uncertainties: Whether experimental verification is mature enough, given logical qubits are still few and small.
Many deserving contributors outside the credited names; selection among the three is contested.
Kitaev's topological contribution might be recognised separately under topological order.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices provide clean, tunable quantum many-body simulators, with the superfluid-to-Mott insulator transition, single-site imaging and a wide range of model Hamiltonians. The impact on many-body physics and quantum simulation is large and lasting, and the experimental control is remarkable.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch and others) supplied the theoretical proposal; Bloch and Greiner carried out the decisive Mott-insulator experiment and developed quantum gas microscopy. Cirac is also credited but is more tied to the broader quantum-simulation proposals. Jaksch, who is not credited, is a key co-author of the Bose-Hubbard proposal, which makes allocation difficult.
assessment.maturity: The field is mature, with many groups reproducing and extending the work over two decades. The overlap with the earlier Bose-Einstein condensation prize and with the other atomic quantum-simulation entries means the actual prize framing would have to be chosen carefully.
uncertainties: Overlap with the other atomic quantum-computation and simulation candidates on the longlist.
Credit omitted for contributors not among the credited names, notably the original Bose-Hubbard proposal.
Whether the application to analogue simulation has delivered decisive new physics so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays combine optical tweezers with blockade interactions to make controllable many-body quantum systems and high-fidelity gates, with quantum simulation of exotic phases and early logical-qubit demonstrations. It is a fast-moving and important platform.
assessment.attribution: Lukin's group built the large programmable arrays and quantum simulators, Browaeys's group did tweezer arrays and spin models, and Saffman made key gate proposals and experiments. The three-way split is plausible but other groups, including Bernien, Endres and Ahn, make this overlapping and uncertain.
assessment.maturity: The main results date from about 2016 to 2023 and are replicated by several groups, yet the field is still moving, and the gate and error-correction results are very recent. Probably somewhat early for a prize.
uncertainties: Rapidly evolving field; the most significant result may not yet be settled.
Many comparable groups with similar claims.
Overlap with the other neutral-atom and trapped-ion candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene revealed flat bands, correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable two-dimensional platform, and opened the whole moire and twistronics field. It is original, widely influential and conceptually clean in its theory prediction.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands at the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group observed the correlated insulator and superconducting phases in 2018, with Cao as lead author. Credit for the experimental discovery is concentrated in Jarillo-Herrero, with Dean and Yacoby in related work who are not in the credited names.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed by many groups within a few years, though the microscopic origin of the superconductivity and correlated states is still debated. This is fast impact, but the physical understanding is not yet settled.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity and correlated phases remains unresolved.
Experimental credit beyond the credited names, including graduate student leads and related groups.
Whether the field is mature enough compared with older candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, combine many atoms with very high Q optical transitions and reach about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty. They enable tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second. Precision metrology of this kind has a strong Nobel tradition.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock; Ye's group pushed the stability and accuracy and built the ultra-stable laser and spectroscopy approach. A two-person prize looks natural, though Hall, Hansch, Wineland and other precision contributors have already been recognised and others including Lemonde could plausibly be added.
assessment.maturity: Independent clocks have been compared and show agreement, and the technology is clearly mature. The redefinition of the second and applications are coming, so the timing is reasonable.
uncertainties: Fit with earlier optical frequency comb and ion-clock prizes.
Others who contributed to lattice-clock development, such as Lemonde or Ludlow, are outside the credited list.
Fundamental-physics results from the clocks so far are null tests, not discoveries.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cooling mechanical oscillators to the quantum ground state and controlling them via radiation-pressure and piezoelectric coupling has made macroscopic mechanical systems a quantum platform. It links closely to superconducting circuits and microwave quantum optics, and tests quantum mechanics at large mass scales.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis demonstrated ground-state cooling and quantum control of a mechanical resonator with a superconducting qubit; Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer made cavity optomechanical cooling and strong coupling. Teufel, Painter and Regal also produced decisive results and are not in the credited names, so the credit is spread.
assessment.maturity: Results are confirmed across several platforms, but they mostly establish capabilities rather than a single discovery changing our understanding. Applications are still emerging and recognition would likely come later.
uncertainties: Diffuse credit among several equally important groups not all listed.
Impact so far is more capability than discovery.
Overlap in theme with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum behaviour.
